utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those just outside the courtroom assisting us. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom I'd like to inform the parties about the position the Chamber takes in respect of 92 bis D or 89 (F) in respect of the production of transcripts in evidence. The Trial Chamber has carefully studied again the position of the Appeals Chamber in the Milosevic case where it became clear that not all categories of written evidence would fall within the scope of 92 bis (A). In respect of the transcripts we would use here, the Chamber considers that -- first of all, that they are not falling outside the scope of 92 bis irrespective of the subject matter. That means that this transcript and the testimony is not about the acts and the conduct of the accused as it should be understood in the case law of this Tribunal. Therefore, for that reason it would fall within the scope of 92 bis. Transcripts are different from written statements to the extent that, first of all, the correct writing down of the words of a witness is not in the hands of an investigator but is the responsibility of the registry. Therefore, an affirmation of the correct text on paper compared to what the witness has said is not an issue. As far as the -- as far as the correctness, that means whether the statement or what has been put on paper is accurate, that means whether it reflects the truth to the best of the knowledge of the witness, is not in a similar way an issue for transcripts as it is for statements since unlike with statements, the witness has given a solemn declaration that he will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So in that respect, there's no need for -- to attest the accuracy. There's no need to confirm that the words are written down in a correct way. So all the formalities we find for 92 bis (A) are, well, not issues as far as transcripts are concerned. As far as the limits are concerned, in this specific case we could say that the transcript, the testimony, is not about the acts and the conduct of the accused, so therefore there is no reason not to apply 92 bis (D). I add to that that this does not mean that transcripts always are covered by Rule 92 bis (D). For example, one could imagine that a witness should be confronted with an inconsistent statement when cross-examined and that a transcript of an earlier testimony could play a role there even if that testimony would be related to the acts and the conduct of the accused, which would exclude that transcript from 92 bis (D) but might bring it within the scope of 89(F). But since that is not the case here, there is no reason for the Chamber not to accept transcripts of the cross-examination of the witness in another case under Rule 92 bis (D). This is perhaps a bit of a long explanation for why the Chamber thinks that in this case the application of 92 bis (D) should be preferred above the more general rule of 89(F). Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, two matters, one I'd like to address concerning that and a procedural matter. If the Defence wishes to adapt that procedure with this witness or future witnesses, we would ask that we be given two weeks' notice of that so we could have a week to respond if there were any objections or something we wanted to raise with regard to what's proposed, because if all that's being offered is the cross-examination, Your Honour, sometimes it -- we feel it may be necessary for the Court also to receive either some portion of the direct testimony that preceded that or the redirect that followed. In this case, Your Honour, I had a chance to look at the cross-examination of Mr. Karabeg from the Brdjanin trial, and we would propose that Your Honours consider the redirect examination that Mr. Cayley conducted of that witness along with the cross-examination, and I have copies of that that I can provide to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to the re-examination question, Your Honour, I think insofar as the re-examination arises from the cross-examination, I have no objection to that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it could have been done live as well. So if it's -- yes. Is it limited to that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we could ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Of course we're trying to find -- oh, yes, no. You had a second issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter relates -- before the witness comes in, Your Honour, there was an issue yesterday regarding one of the exhibits for our first witness regarding the translation, and Mr. Gaynor is ready to address that. I think we've discovered what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, perhaps if you'd briefly explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. The exhibit in question is P95. It was a record by the Cantonal Court in Bihac about an exhumation which took place on the 28th of October, 1998. The top right-hand corner of the English translation of the B/C/S original, Your Honour, drew our attention to the fact that it says handwritten: 9.480. On inspection of the original, it appears that that annotation does not exist. We suspect that that number refers to an exhibit number from the Brdjanin trial. This exhibit was also an exhibit in the Brdjanin trial. Therefore, we propose that Exhibit P95.1, which is the English translation of this document, be replaced with this translation which is the same translation without the annotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any comments, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. There is no objection to that course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the translation is then tendered and is also then admitted in the new version. It is exactly the same document but without the translation of handwriting on the top of it, yes. Then, if there are no further issues, Mr. Usher could you please escort Mr. Karabeg into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The examination-in-chief will now continue. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, I think we had just talked about the situation in Sanski Most municipality in early April of 1992, and that was a time in which you told us that the SDS and the municipal assembly was trying to get on the agenda the issue of Sanski Most becoming a Serbian municipality and joining the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, and you told us about a conversation you had with Mr. Vrkes about that. I want to ask you, did that issue ever get officially voted on in the Assembly in Sanski Most, the issue of joining ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, there was a vote on whether to put it on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that vote?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal was not accepted, the proposal to be -- place the issue on the agenda, because the SDS members wanted to break at that point. And then it was decided that the commission should be set up consisting of various representatives of the political parties. They tried to resolve the issue, to have the Assembly continue with its work. However, this never happened, and it was the last session of the municipal assembly of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what date that last session was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that it must have been either on the 6th or the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to have you shown an exhibit. The next item, I believe, if we can have a number. It will be for a document dated 25 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P103.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And actually, Mr. Karabeg, there are two documents together here. One is dated 25 March 1992, described as Reasons, and one dated 3 April 1992, called a Decision. And I believe you've seen this document before when you testified previously here at the Tribunal. Do you recall having seen that document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of that document in 1992 at the time it appears to have been written?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I saw this document for the first time two years ago when I attended a trial here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that document, the first one dated the 25th of March, it appears that the Serbian authorities have decided that all Serbian territories in Sanski Most municipality will be part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the document dated the 3rd of April is a decision that the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most will be part of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see, the way they did it was illegal. I mean, they were doing this illegally, but we had this legal Assembly that took place on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been asked a simple question, that is whether that document is or is not as indicated, and the answer is yes, and the witness has now gone on to answer a further question that was not asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, if a witness thinks that there's something important to be added, we usually let him go if it does not go too far away from the original question. Of course, he could not start telling a story about a totally different matter. I would first leave it to Mr. Hannis whether further elaboration of the witness fits into what he would like to ask the witness. If so, he doesn't have to interrupt the witness and ask him the question he is already answering. So therefore, I would leave it, first of all, to counsel who is at that moment examining the witness, but I expect counsel to stop a witness if he just explores areas which are not relevant at that moment. And of course, some control over what then happens should be exercised. This would be valid for both parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I think you told us you were not aware of this at the time it occurred even though you were president of the Executive Board in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you started to say before that this decision, in your opinion, was illegal. Could you explain to us why you have that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me address the Court at this point. I wish to say that it is very difficult and almost impossible for me to answer with a simple yes or no. There are always things that I feel need to be added, and I think this is the reason why I have been called upon to testify before the Tribunal, so that the truth can be established. Now, when I said that I had seen the document for the first time two years ago when I attended a trial here, the trial which was conducted against Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic, they did this illegally. What they tried to do legally was to attempt to place on the agenda of the Assembly the issue itself, and that was that. However, they were not successful in that. They wanted then a commission to be established. A commission was indeed established, but it could not reach a good solution because we non-Serbs, at that point, requested that the issue of reunification of Sanski Most with Bihac be placed on the agenda, and neither of the proposals were accepted. So the Assembly ceased to function. So legal organs were not respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, after this last session of the Sanski Most Assembly, in your written statement, I think in paragraphs 15 and 16, you talk about the split of the police force in Sanski Most. Can you tell us how that came about?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Assembly stopped functioning, the representative of the SDS went about establishing municipal organs of the Sanski Most municipality in their own way. First they tried to do it with the police. Vlado Vrkes, the president of the local branch of the SDS, talked to the people from the police and said that he wanted a meeting to be convened, a meeting which would be attended by all of the police officers or members of the Milicija, as we called them at the time. All police officers from the Sanski Most municipalities, those who were attached to the Sanski Most police, representatives of the parties as well. And it was said at that meeting that all police officers should wear Serb insignia and that a Serbian flag bearing four Ss should be hoisted at the building of the police, and that all police officers should sign an oath of loyalty to the Serbian police. Now, at that meeting, none of the Serbs accepted to sign --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karabeg. I see something in your answer just now I wanted to ask you about before I forgot. You said that all police officers should sign an oath of loyalty to the Serbian police? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I'm confused. But I thought in your written statement --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is cross-examining his own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first have a look at the written statement before I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would direct you to paragraph 15 in the English version. The fourth line talks about the loyalty pledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 15 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 15, the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. May I ask you one question? The declaration of loyalty, could you expand on that a tiny little bit more? How was that done? What was the text? Do you know any more specifics about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the actual text, but I can only assume what it was. They said that a loyalty oath or declaration should be signed, which means that you sign to respect the regulations of the Sanski Most municipality, that you will respect rules and regulations when it comes to the police at the level of the Autonomous Region, which means all the changes illegally. The legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to -- expected to sign loyalty to those who wished to topple all this and to work illegally, unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Perhaps you could move to your next subject or -- I think the matter has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, I'm sorry I interrupted you I think before you finished your answer about that meeting. Was there something additional you wanted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I wanted to tell you was this: On that day, none of the policemen or militiamen as they were called who worked, who were on duty, stated that they wished to sign this declaration of loyalty and that they wished to work under the Republika Srpska, that they did not wish to wear the four-S insignia except for one young Croat who said he'd have to accept to sign that declaration of loyalty because he lived in Banja Luka and that he was sorry that he had to do that, but he had to accept this. So as this -- nobody accepted this pledge of loyalty, then Vlado Vrkes gave a deadline of, I think, 48 hours to think about this, the acceptance of this declaration of loyalty. The 48 hours expired. Nobody accepted to sign the declaration of loyalty, and so the legal policemen were not allowed access to the police station. They were sent away and dismissed from their jobs by these illegal people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, in paragraph 16 of your written statement, you indicated that Mr. Vrkes gave this ultimatum about signing the loyalty oath and wearing the insignia, and you further on say: "The Serbs said we belong to Banja Luka region" --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object at this point. I mean, the statement is in evidence. If Mr. Hannis wants to add additional matters to the evidence, it really should come from the mouth of the witness, not from reading out his statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the statement is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no idea what question will follow here, whether he would like to ask, whether -- well, whatever question would come at first, rather -- I mean, I do understand that Mr. Hannis takes the statement which is in evidence to further explore any matter, then it very much depends on what he'd like to know, whether it's admissible to give this introduction yes or no. So at first I'd like Mr. Hannis to put the question to the witness, but if you would then please wait to answer that question so that further objections, if necessary, can be made. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 -- 16 - I'm sorry, Mr. Karabeg - it says that: "The Serbs said we belong to the Banja Luka region, we belong to Serb Krajina. They said that if you do not do this, there is no way to protect non-Serbs from extremists." Can you recall specifically who told you that, which one of the Serbs said that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes said that, and President Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they explain why they were of the opinion that there was no way protect you from the extremists?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see. It was a period where one could feel the worst was coming, and the SDS had extended arm. Sometimes they called them the Serb armed forces. Sometimes they were called the Serb armed forces, this extended arm. And they did evil on the territory of Sanski Most municipality to the non-Serb population. They sort of said that they were extremist Serbs and that they could wield no influence on them and that the ones that perpetrated these acts could not be stopped, whereas in actual fact they did what they did pursuant to their instructions, all the evil things they did. And on the other hand, they said that they weren't able to defend us from those extremist Serbs which they actually put against us, set against us. And it was during this period of time that from the war fields, from Pakrac, when UNPROFOR arrived, the 6th Krajina Brigade was sent back fully equipped, under arms, fully equipped with weapons in the Sanski Most municipality, and they also committed evil acts. They would get drunk. They would shoot around and do things like that. So that was what happened. Those were the people who were supposed to protect us or, rather, they said that they couldn't protect us from people like that. And they said that they wouldn't protect us from the people that actually they issued orders to and were in command of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you to explain a little bit for us about what you refer to as this extended arm. How big a group of people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to wait for an objection from the Defence for me to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That was -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that I should wait awhile to hear the question from the Prosecution and then the objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the last question. If there are any specific instructions to be given, I'll give them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would like to make one point. It's been called forth, Your Honour, just in relation to that last question. Again, whilst of course the witness wishes to explain, the answer was not entirely responsive to the question. So -- and went on for a couple of paragraphs, didn't specifically actually answer the question that Mr. Hannis asked. I'm just wondering if perhaps the witness could be reminded to actually answer the specific question that's asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked in the last question by Mr. Hannis whether they did explain why they were not -- why there was no way to protect you from the extremists. In your answer, I think you gave your own opinion about why they couldn't protect you or why they said they couldn't protect you, but the specific question was about what they gave as an explanation. Could you tell us whether they gave any explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not wish to protect us. To us, they said they wanted to protect us, but actually they did not wish to protect us because they had these people as the extended arm to do the evil and create chaos in the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not wish to. They told us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to our eyes that they did want to protect us, but in actual fact they did not wish to protect us because they forced these people to commit evil deeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So their answer was, "We'd like to protect you but we can't." Did they give any specific reason why they said they couldn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To accept reality, to accept -- they said, "Accept reality, accept the Serbian region of Sanski Most and the Bosnian Krajina region and then we will protect you." That was what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they said on the one hand, "We would like to protect you but we only can," and of course "can" has different meanings, "do this if you accept the reality." Is that what they told you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loyalty, yes. If we accept loyalty, if we accept Republika Srpska and if we accept that Sanski Most be proclaimed Serbian Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell me how many -- if you know, how many people approximately in this extended arm of the Serbian defence forces that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were up to 50 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were those men? Were they local or were they from somewhere outside Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all local people, all born in Sanski Most, all people from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the leader of this unit or this group was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We thought at the time that the leader of the group, of that group was Dusko Savija. However, we later learnt that all the time it was actually Tomo Delic who took part with us in all our negotiations, and he always said he wished to protect us from the group whereas in actual fact he was head of the group the whole time. He was a well-to-do stonemason from Sanski Most, from Krogora [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just for clarification I recall in your testimony in Brdjanin that there is an acronym or an abbreviation for this group Serbian defence forces. I just want to be sure we're talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to make sure we're talking about the same thing with regard to the Serbian defence forces. There is an acronym referred to in your prior testimony, SOS. Is that the group you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand from your written statement that you left Sanski Most on the 19th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of April, 1992. That was when I left my work post. They forbid me to come in as president of the Executive Board to enter the building. Or more exactly, not the 19th, it was actually the 20th. The 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, between the 11th of April when the police force went through this reorganisation you described and when you left, were you the SDA and HDZ still trying to negotiate with the SDS about how to run the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did try, but they didn't wish to have any contact with us after the 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But between the 11th of April and the 19th or 20th of April, were you still have talks with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were. That's right. We would have talks every day, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you briefly summarise what were the -- what were the topics of your negotiation? What was being proposed by each side?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see: We asked that the legal organs should function, the legal organs in the Sanski Most municipality, meaning the police and the other organs of power and authority, and when they asked the loyalty pledge to be signed for the police, the Milicija, and that insignia be worn in conformity with that, they took over the police building and did not allow the legally elected policemen to go to their workplaces. And we said, "There is a lot of room in that building. So there is the part of the building where you are, and there is the other part which houses the Territorial Defence and the secretariat of the Territorial Defence. So can we be accommodated there and can the police be accommodated there, in that portion of the building?" They said that that was impossible, that the building belonged to them, that they would keep it for themselves and that allegedly we could think about the municipality building. Now, on the 17th of April, when we had the last discussion about the police force, we decided to go to the police building. I myself did because I was President of the Executive Board. So I went to my office. I called the party president Redzo Kurbegovic to come, and in the meantime I was called up on the telephone by the chief of police, Mr. Burnic, the komandir. He was a Bosniak and he asked me, "Where are we policemen going to have to go, because we are now in the fire brigade centre." And I said, "Well, come over to the municipality building and that's where we're going to stay, so we can all gather there together, all the workers of the organs of management can gather there, the non-Serbs, I mean, the non-Serb inhabitants," and that's what happened. We started rallying in the municipality building, but actually they didn't like that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there if I may, Mr. Karabeg. Did they have some specific proposals about how to divide the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was, you see: They came out with the proposal that the municipality should be divided and that the municipality should be divided according to the branches and services. The municipality building had two floors, two stories, so that we should divide this, but the proposal wasn't that one side should have one floor and the other side should have the other floor but to cut the building vertically in half, so that half the building belonged to one side and half to the other, and we agreed to this in principle. What happened was that a third proposal was put on the table; that is to say, that the building should be left to them and that we should leave across the Sana River to the other bank of the River Sana and take up accommodation in the administration building there which belonged to the Sipad company. We said, well, don't make us go all that way because it would create a new problem. Sipad, that is Sipad's administration building, and 90 per cent of their workers were Serbs by ethnicity, and we were sure that we would have problems with those employees. So we realised that they were actually trying to expel us and force us into new problems, from one problem to another, from the frying-pan into the fire, so to speak. So we didn't accept that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you if they had in addition to this proposal regarding the -- the governmental authorities, was there a proposal also to divide the town in the business and residential areas and, if so, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, that's right. They did have that proposal that Sanski Most should be divided. Not by the districts but by streets, depending on the inhabitants, the majority population in that street. So if a street was mostly inhabited by Serbs, it would be a Serb street. In streets inhabited by the non-Serbs, it would belong to our street -- the street would be ours. We said that that was absolutely impossible, and then they even went so far as to propose Ruzic Mirko and Boro Savanovic, two men who worked in the town planning department, and they brought in a map of the Sanski Most municipality with certain proposals along those lines to divide up the town, but we said that this was quite impossible, that it was not feasible at all, and that it couldn't be done. And that's -- but their proposal stood, and they actually didn't need any proposal because they took over the whole of Sanski Most and the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you on the 17th of April, where were you physically located along with the non-Serb police?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, we were in the building of the Sanski Most municipality from 1.00 on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you receive any request or demand from the SDS on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you how it was. When we entered the building, we had those talks and negotiations, and this mostly went during those few days, that is to say, the 17th was a Friday, and on the Saturday the 18th and Sunday the 19th. And after that they put forward their proposal to divide up the building, to divide it in half. We accepted. When we accepted that, then they said, well, it shouldn't be cut in half because the building was on the right bank of the Sana River and that we should go to the administration building of the Sipad company across the river, across the bridge, the other side of the Sana River, to leave them the whole building. So the talks -- those were the talks we had and the discussions we had over those three days. And when the ultimatum followed on the 19th, that is to say, on Sunday, in the evening, sometime around a quarter to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ultimatum and who did it come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is how it was: When we were in the building, Nedeljko Rasula, the President of the Assembly, called Vlado Sabica [as interpreted] and told him we should leave the building and that we should lay down our arms in front of the building and that nothing would happen to us. We would not be harmed. If we failed to do so, then we might not walk the earth any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second to correct something in the transcript. Sir, who did Mr. Rasula call? Could you give us the name of the person that Rasula called? Because it appears in the transcript as Vlado Sabica, and I think you told me before that it was someone else.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suada Sabica. Sabic. Suad Sabic. Vlado Suad Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there a time by which you had to leave the building and lay down your arms?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 2200 hours. When Suad Sabic arrived and told us of the conversation he had had with Rasula, we had a meeting. However, in the meantime, one of the policemen called us, and he saw through the window, as it's a hill, he saw a column approaching with about 30 vehicles, and it was night-time. The vehicles were lit up. They had lights. And we assumed straight away -- we were 100 per cent certain that this was in fact a column of soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade who were stationed in Luka Palanka which is 25 kilometres away, lead by Pukovnik Basara. And when we saw this, we realised that there was nothing for us, that we had to leave the building of the Sanski Most municipality by the back door. Most of us went to the village of Sehovac, and a small portion, seven or eight, went to Gornja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened at the municipality building after you left it that evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we left that evening, the building was shelled with rifle grenades. Bombs were thrown. Grenades were thrown. There was shooting in the building. Zoljas were used, handheld rocket launchers, automatic rifles. And the next day when I entered the municipality building when General Talic was arriving, I used this opportunity to take a look at my office, but it was all bullet-riddled, completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute, and I want to show you an exhibit, a document now, dated the 20th of April. And I want to ask your comment on something that's in this document purportedly from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality. And this is to the Chief of Staff of the Banja Luka Public Security Service and the Serbian news agency, and I want to read the third paragraph and ask you a question about that. It says: "It's the opinion of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most that force had to be used in order to free the Sanski Most municipal building from armed formations of the extremist wing of the SDA leadership. Long and exhausting negotiations simply did not bear fruit." Can you tell me, Mr. Karabeg, what is being referred to as the extremist wing of the SDA leadership in that document, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: If there was an extremist wing with respect to the SDA, then that would be me, and I'm sitting here. The President of the Executive Board of the legally elected organ of the legally elected government, the police or Milicija legally elected once again, and now these para-illegals wish to portray themselves as being legal and lawful representing something that was illegal and unlawful against us who were performing our functions legally, but they were preventing us in doing that. And even these negotiations. They prolonged them for such a long time and gave us some sort -- they said that they agreed and tried to win us over, but in fact they were leading us into a less and less favourable situation and they succeeded in doing that ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, I don't think I got an exhibit number for that document. Could that be given the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Exhibit number P104.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I think you said before that you did come back into town the next day, on April 20th. Can you tell us why you came back, how that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, this is how it happened: On the 19th of April, at about 2200, we left the town hall, the municipality building, having been forced to do so, and went to Sehovci where we spent the entire night. And the next morning at about five minutes past 7.00, the president of the municipality, Nedeljko Rasula called us and he talked to Suad Sabic again, to whom he said that Momir -- General Momir Talic should arrive at 11.00 [as interpreted] in the municipality building together with his associates and that he wanted to talk with us about the current problems. We accepted that, and then he said, "I will send a group of policemen at quarter to 12.00 so that you can be escorted." And we told him that we did not want their escorts but that we wanted our police officers who had been legally appointed to act as our escorts. And he said that there could be no question about it, but then he called us a little later again, and he said that it was okay, that we could come with our police officers but that we should be there at 12.00 so that we could proceed with the talks and negotiations. So we got there escorted by our police. Suad Sabic, Anto Tunjic on behalf of the HDZ, Kurbegovic. We came to the Sanski Most town hall where we were received and finally taken to the office of the president, Mr. Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about that. Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town hall, in the municipality building, in the office of the then president of the Serbian Sanski Most, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the same building you had left just the day before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you described for us some of the damage you observed to the building on that day. Did you observe any armed formation around the building and, if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you there were armed formations around the building. As far as I could notice, those were members of the police, as far as I could tell. And the president of the party, Mr. Vlado Vrkes, and this was quite telling, this is what we noticed in particular, entered the building in a new military uniform, wearing a pistol stuck at his belt. And we could also see as we were entering the building that the building had been damaged. I used this opportunity when I arrived to see my office, because it is located before the office of the president, Rasula, so I took a peek and I realised that the office had been riddled with bullets. Hand grenades had been thrown into the basement. We could see that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who else attended this meeting other than the ones you've described already? Was there a representative from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Momir Talic, the late General Momir Talic, Colonel Hasagic, Major Zeljaja were there. I don't remember others, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, the discussion resolved around the situation that had arisen in the meantime, the fact that we had been in the municipality building, that an ultimatum had been issued, that the municipality had actually been attacked, that local business premises had been blown up, that the soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade had erected barricades and checkpoints, that many of the soldiers walked around in an inebriated state and opened fire, that the situation, generally speaking, was chaotic. General Talic listened to what we had to say, and we adopted a certain number of conclusions regarding this issue. The first one was that checkpoints should be removed, that legally elected organs should take up their offices again, that an end should be put to blowing up the local business premises, and General Talic accepted our proposals as conclusions of the meeting. At the time, it was possible to address the public over the radio, the local radio station, and we proposed, we suggested that he should read out our conclusions over the radio. However, the director of the local station, Mr. Orlovic, said that it was technically unfeasible. When we disagreed, we also suggested that General Talic could simply pick up the telephone and be put through to the local radio station and that these conclusions could be read out and broadcast over the radio. General Talic said, however, that he had no time for that, that he should go back to Banja Luka. But there was one thing that we agreed upon, and that is that we would meet again in the municipal building that same evening at about 11.00 [as interpreted] to continue talking about the -- all of these issues and to adopt further conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I arrived outside the building, but the building, the municipal building was surrounded and blocked by members of the police. There were hedgehogs around it, transport vehicles, a number of police officers outside the building, and I realised it was no longer possible for me to enter the building of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I want to talk for a minute about the discussions you had and the conclusions reached with General Talic, and to do that I want to show you something in a document that I would like to have marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like to explain a little bit about this next item. This is a item that's purported to be the diary of the Nedeljko Rasula, the president of the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most. That was item that was introduced into evidence in the Brdjanin case. And for Your Honours to make some conclusions about this, I think it's important to consider the 92 bis evidence of a number of the Sanski Most witnesses who talk in more detail about this particular item than this witness did or can, particularly the testimony of Adil Draganovic. But for now, I would like to read out one small passage from the diary relating to that meeting, and later on there's one other passage I want to read to the witness and ask him to comment on related to his arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P105.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the first section that I want to go to in the English begins at the bottom of page 16 and the ERN is 01104343 and carries on over to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karabeg, for your reference, I know the diary appears to be in handwritten Cyrillic. Do you read Cyrillic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, capital letters. I can read capital Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm a bit confused. You say it begins at page 16 and the ERN, last four digits, is 4343 whereas it is 4344 in my English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe there's a difference in numbering in the copy I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have something marked on the bottom of page 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it the comments of General Talic? I'm looking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to refer to General Talic's concluding remarks, that's on the bottom of page 17 in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: ERN number 4345.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I -- I have a different number on the copy I have, but that is the portion I want, the concluding remarks of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But wouldn't it be wise that you're working from the same version as the Chamber does because otherwise we'll have to check every single letter. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that copy, Your Honour. There appears to be a difference in the page breaks. I'm now working from the same copy that Your Honours have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then perhaps I can ask for one further clarification, that is my first page has two ERN numbers on it. On the top it's 01104328, and on the bottom it is 01104329. Oh, let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think this copy, there is more than one ERN per page in some cases. It's not a one-to-one match-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that, although it switches after number 10, and in the original that's still on one page of the -- let's see whether we could follow you on the bottom of page 17, ERN number three last digits, 4345.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I want to read you something and ask you a question. Here in the document it says: "General Talic concluding remarks, reach agreement but without undue delay. The police -- military police from Prijedor shall remain and if need be from Banja Luka. We do not recognise the paramilitary formations. We're not allowing barricades to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be put up. The JNA will guarantee the peace of the citizenry and the security of property. We're asking for your help." And then it says: "Don't call anyone for help otherwise you will have Kupres, Bosanski Brod, Vukovar." Do you recall General Talic makes these remarks during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you understand the remark about Kupres, Bosanski Brod and Vukovar to mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you how it was. We took it to mean, to refer to the situation in those cities, that Sanski Most would also become a destroyed city, a scene of the conflict, and that is what he had in mind - at least that's what we thought - when he alluded to Vukovar and the situation in that city, the city that had seen a lot of destruction and many conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After that meeting, you indicated that there were some proposals that had been put and agreed upon, including removing the checkpoints. Were those carried out in accordance with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. Quite the contrary. The situation grew worse. We proposed that we should meet again at 1800 at the municipal building, but that meeting never took place, for instance. But there is one other thing that I have to mention. That day when we parted with General Talic, I talked to him a little, and I told him that he had seen for himself what the situation was. And I also said that I did not believe that the meeting would take place that evening, but General Talic gave me his telephone number, and he told me that I could call him at any time of the day should the situation deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you call him?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we did not meet on the 20th of May at 6.00 p.m., the next day the situation did not change, and then on Wednesday at 9.00, 9.30, I called General Talic on the number that he had given me, and it was rather strange that I was able to get him 10 to 15 seconds later. I didn't have to wait at all. And I told him that Rasula was not accepting any of the conclusions that we had adopted. He raised his voice, and then he swore at Rasula. And at that moment, I think I believed that -- I think it was a Thursday, and it was the liberation day of Banja Luka. I was watching the news, and the breaking news was the ceremony that was taking place on that day. I saw Talic sitting in the front row together with Karadzic. I believe Krajisnik was also there together with Biljana Plavsic and others, and because of that I only laughed at what he had said. If I may please finish. I laughed and I said, "These guys are lying to us. They are only pretending that they're trying to help us, but actually they're not accepting any of our proposals." Because this was quite a blow for me, the fact that I had seen the general there at that ceremony, the general who had given us his promises the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for one clarification first. You earlier indicated that the second meeting on the same day would take place at 11.00 at night, whereas you then twice said that it would take place at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, there is the period of time between the 17th and the 19th of April, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. At 2200 hours on the 19th of April, we were forced to leave the building of the municipality and went to Sehovci. On the 20th they summoned us to come to the meeting which it can place at noon and lasted until 3.00 in the afternoon with General Talic, at which meeting we agreed that we should meet again at 1800 hours with Rasula and others at the building of the Sanski Most municipality to continue with our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the transcript reads, I may draw the attention of the parties to page 26, line 6. It's written down as your testimony, but -- and I'll read it to you. "General Talic said, however, that he had no time for that, that he should go back to Banja Luka, but there was one thing that we agreed upon and that is that we would meet again in the municipal building that same evening at about 11.00 to continue talking about all of these issues and to adopt further conclusions." So you in the beginning -- I don't know whether it is a translation mistake. You said 11.00, at least we read that it was translated to us as 11.00, whereas you said later two times and now you confirm that it was 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, no. This never took place nor was it possible for me to state that. Just a second. So that we -- I mean, General Talic said that he had no time, and at 3.00 on the 20th, he left Sanski Most and went to Banja Luka, but the idea was for us who stayed behind to meet again at 1800 at the municipal building in order to continue the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to clarify there must have been a mistake, whatever mistake, about 11.00. We have some time restraints, and you earlier explained that whenever you would like to add something you would like to do so, but nevertheless, I would like you to follow a bit more the questions. If any further elaboration is needed, you'll certainly hear additional questions put in that respect, but I would like to leave it mainly to counsel where to focus on, and if there is any specific issue you'd like to raise, you always can ask me whether you can add something. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was that the last time you had a conversation with General Talic was that phone call when you complained about Mr. Rasula's failure to follow up on the agreements of 20 April? Was that the last time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there someone else from the JNA that became the point of contact for you and the SDA after that last contact with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did Colonel Basara take any action in the community of Sanski Most around that time talking about what the JNA could and would do to try to help the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is what happened. I did not take part in the talks with Basara. The so-called Patriotic League was established at the time, which consisted of the representatives of the leftist parties, and I know that Fuad Kurbegovic told me that he had talked to Basara at that meeting, and that he said that he would see to it that the situation in the Sanski Most municipality improves and that he would protect the non-Serb population. And Suad expressed his gratitude for that line of thinking, and he said that he had suggested that Colonel Basara would be declared as a honourary citizen of Sanski Most, but nothing came of that. No promises were -- were made, nor was he ever declared an honourary citizen of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you talk about that I think in paragraph 60 of your written statement, where you also say that Colonel Basara was promising that he would, "Deal with extremists in the SDS and SOS." Did he deal with the extremists in the SDS and SOS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned before the SOS. Can you tell us the names of some of the local Serbs from Sanski Most who were a part of that unit? You mentioned a couple already, but do you -- can you name any others?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Mudrinic, Dusko Savija, Tomo Delic, Dane Kajtez, also known as Daniluska. I don't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you yourself were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were you arrested and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested at home, and it was the people that I just identified that arrested me. They were led by Dusan Mudrinic, also known as Medeni. Then there were others as well. They came in two vehicles. I remember Mico Krunic, a retired police officer who was there, then this man by the nickname of Lasta. I don't know his family name. I don't remember others, but I know that there were eight of them and that they had come in two vehicles, in an old Mercedes and a Lada Niva and that they were fully armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they wear any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did. They wore camouflage uniforms, but some also wore the old Milicija or police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to the police station. Medeni told me that Rasula and other police officers wanted to see me and have an interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be a good time for the break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This would be a suitable time for the break. We will have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you may proceed. Do you have any idea on how much time you'd still take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe I will take more than an hour to finish with this witness. We had him originally scheduled for four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. And we are of course we expected to gain some time on the 89(F). Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I think you still have in front of you Exhibit P105, and it's turned to a page that I want to read something from and ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in the English I believe this is page number 39 or ERN 01104365.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karabeg, on your document --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Hannis proceeds, if we could also have the B/C/S number so that Mr. Krajisnik can turn to the right page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was just starting to read that number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the 25th of May at least, so if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And the ERN for the B/C/S is 00379462. And it's the right-hand page, and we're talking about an entry that is for the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There are four items listed. Number three talks about the disarmament plan and its beginning, and number four is pre-empting enemy operations. A is arrest of leaders, and B is detention facilities. Item 4 is discussed in further detail below. It talks about take into custody Adil Draganovic and arrest Redzo Kurbegovic, Mirzet Karabeg and others. And, Mr. Karabeg, you told us you were arrested on the 25th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during April and May 1992, were you aware of any disarmament activity taking place in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we, up until the 11th of April, 1992, or thereabouts, until the SDS put forward its proposal according to which the police should sign the loyalty oath and bear Serbian insignia of the Autonomous Province of Banja Luka, we had joint distribution of arms from the Territorial Defence, and members of the reserve force of the Territorial Defence, the reservists and the reserve policemen were issued arms. We had joint collection points in the municipality up until the arrival of the 6th Krajina Brigade to the Sanski Most municipality and its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Karabeg, maybe I wasn't clear. Were there any activities --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was just going to address that issue and to continue. And through the media, by the Serb police and the leadership of the SDS, it was -- the non-Serbs were asked to return their weapons that they had in their possession, and people accepted this because they knew what could happen to them should they fail to return those weapons. And what happened was that they returned that legally issued -- those legally issued weapons to which they -- which they had been given. And I myself as President of the Executive Board had, by virtue of office, in my safe, I had an automatic and 200 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you surrender your weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last thing I want to read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Under item 3 of the disarmament plan in Exhibit P105 it indicates that captured civilians to be used for exchanges. Sir, were you eventually exchanged after your arrest and detention?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 31st of October, 1992. From the Manjaca camp, but we're talking about the beginning, the 25th of May. So I experienced and lived through a great deal and received a lot of beatings to boot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about that now. Now I'm finished with that document, sir, so you won't need to refer to that any more. I think right before the break you told us you were arrested and taken to the police station in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before we continue, I see that you have paid attention to two specific pages of this document. Of course I cannot exclude the wider context becomes relevant at a later stage. If you would limit it to these two pages, I wonder whether we have to admit into evidence the whole of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be seeking to admit the whole diary before we finish with Sanski Most, because it is talked about by several the witness or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we get other relevant parts as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, when you were taken to the police station, what happened to you there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested, I was told that I would go for an informative talk, as they put it, and I expected to see the president, Nedeljko Rasula, and Vlado Vrkes, and that it really would be a talk. So I went to the police building, but when I got there they told me to sit down in the hallway and a 15 minutes later somebody came to fetch me, one of the policemen, I know his first name was Kuzmo. And he said that I should take the laces out of my shoes and give him my belt, my trouser belt, and some other items I had on me, to leave them behind, and he escorted me to the prison, the police prison cell, and I was put in cell number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other people in cell number 2 when you were first placed there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When I got there, I found three other persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show you a photograph. And could this be given the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P106.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is a picture of, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a picture of the building, of what was the police station at the time and the Territorial Defence and the defence secretariat, their premises, and the front entrance and the police building, the front entrance from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us where on that photograph the front entrance to the police department is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the front entrance, the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is now. It still exists, that entrance does, and so does the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'd like to show you another photograph right now. If it could be given the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just for the record, the witness pointed to the front of the higher four-storey part of the building on the left of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because otherwise people would have to consult the video to order to know what the witness pointed at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P107.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, how big was that cell that you were placed in approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The size of the cell was two by three metres. Two metres wide or three or four metres long, but I think it was three metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you take a look at Exhibit P107 on the ELMO next to you right now and tell us if you recognise what that's a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the cells in the prison in which we were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that cell number 2 that you were kept in or can you tell?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this could be cell number 2. I think it could be cell number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long were you kept in that cell? How many days were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in this cell from the 25th of May, 1992, and I said previously that that was up to the 6th of June, but I made a mistake, and I was there until the 9th of June in actual fact, when I was sent to the Betonirka company where I spent from the 9th of June to the 7th of July. And then I was returned on the 7th of July and stayed there until the 28th of August in this cell, in this particular cell number 2 again in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during those two separate occasion or those two separate periods of time that you were kept in this cell at the prison, what was the maximum number of men inside that cell at one time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, all the time non-stop there were seven us in the cell, but on one particular night there were 14 of us, and that was when it was best they transferred seven more to cell number 2 from cell number 1. But we were happy to see one another and to hear each other, because we were lying one cell next to another with a wall dividing us. So we were actually happy that these people were placed into our cell because it gave us a chance to talk to then, because when we were let out for breakfast and lunch, they would let out the prisoners from cell number 1, and then they would take them back and cell number 2 would go out for breakfast and lunch and then so on and so forth down the cells. So they never let us out together. They would let us out individually from each particular cell. But at that time there were 14 of us, and of course although we didn't sleep the entire night, we were happy to be able to talk to one another the whole night. But as I say, the regular inmates, there were seven of us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were the people that were kept in that cell with you? Did you know them? What was their ethnicity? Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew all those people, all of them. They were all citizens of the Sanski Most municipality, non-Serbs, of non-Serb ethnicity, which means Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were the conditions like other than -- you've described what the size was and how many people were in there, but what were the conditions as far as food and sanitation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just say that I wasn't able to recognise this cell straight away, but I remember, because on the opening here, the aperture, there was a piece of tin plate that -- with holes in it, with very small holes for the air to come in, small ventilation holes, but otherwise there was this tin plate. And they would let us out in the morning for five or ten minutes, usually five, sometimes ten, to have breakfast, and then they would let us out for lunch at about 3.00 or 4.00, once again five or ten minutes. And all the rest of the time we spent in the cell. And when we were in the cell, the conditions were what they were. We had to take it, make do with what we had. But of course we were always beaten, all of us, and we were given orders to beat each other. Somebody would always come into the cell, and somebody would always find a reason to have us beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what provisions were there for sanitation and keeping yourselves clean?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the sanitation was concerned and sanitary conditions, this is how it was: We had a WC within this compound with a tap, a water tap, and when we were allowed out for breakfast or lunch, we would use that opportunity to come back as soon as possible to wash ourselves and to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your five or ten minutes for breakfast and lunch, what kind of food and how much did you get?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be given -- well, the food was the remains of what the reservists had had to eat, what was left behind after the reserve policemen. So they would have their meals before us, and what was left, we would eat their leftovers. Well, actually, we didn't see whether it was their leftovers, but the food was always cold and watered down. And as far as bread was concerned, we could only dream about eating bread. We had a very thin slice now and again in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were the people that were guarding you while you were kept here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were guarded by mostly policemen. They were mostly policemen, as we called them, the militiamen, but policemen, yes, mostly. And we were guarded around the clock. They had three shifts. But there was another characteristic feature. Entrance into this prison -- the entrance to the prison incorporated a large steel door which was locked. So this large steel door had to be unlocked and opened for anybody to reach us, to reach the part we were in. And then we were all locked up individually, seven by seven, in the individual cells. And they had steel doors or iron Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. doors as well. And there was a small aperture, a small opening on the door. You could open it to let some air in, but they kept closing off this opening, this small window. So there was no possibility of having a bit of ventilation through that small opening. And we started to suffocate from the lack of air. And one day towards evening we were taken outside the cells, and the tin plate that had the small holes in it was blocked up -- was taken down, and this left the window, which was open, so we were happy, because we thought that was for our own health, but we realised that there was a visit from the International Red Cross, and that's why they had taken down this perforated tin plate and let a little air come in through the window. But as soon as they had left and the visit was over, they put it back in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that there were beatings while you were there. Who were the people that were beating you and what organisation did they belong to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assumed that they were all policemen. Most of the people guarding us beat us as well, most of them did. Specifically, let me give you an example. When we were let out for lunch on one occasion, I stayed back in the toilet. I spent a longer time in the toilet and spent time washing. And when I went back to the cell, I saw there was nobody in the cell, and the policeman said to me, "They're not here. You go out." So I stepped out, and I saw five of them standing up against a wall with their hands behind their backs and their heads lowered. The policeman said, "Now, here's a baton, and you must give -- hit everybody five times, give everybody five blows." What could I do? I started beating them. When I had finished, the policeman said to me, "That's not the way you do it. Fuck your balija mother," and then he took the baton from me and began beating me. And then he said, "Now you stand up against the wall," and he took another one out and he told the other man to beat the rest us. And so he repeated this with all six of us, so we all had to take turns in beating each other and then finally he beat us all together, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, who were the other five people that you beat? I'm not asking for names but ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks and one Croat by the name of Franjo. Franjo Ilicic was his name. So six of us in the cell at that point in time, cell number 2. But that was just one example.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your next place of detention. You said you were -- for the first time you were there from May 25th to June the 9th and then you went to Betonirka. I'd like to show you a photograph. If it could be given the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P108.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Betonirka was before the fighting started in Sanski Most? What kind of facility was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Betonirka was in fact a set of garages for official vehicles belonging to the Splonum company which was a section of Betonirka, Sanakerm, and there this was a department of the Betonirka firm. So they were a garage complex but not finished, incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit P108 and tell us what that's a picture of.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, I can see the administration building of the Betonirka company and also the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you describe and tell us which of those buildings is the administration building and where it is on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. It is at the entrance to the Betonirka compound. This is the administrative building. And this is the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I believe for the administration building he pointed to the white building on the left side of the photograph, and he indicated the police building as the -- what appears to be a three-storey building on the right edge of the photograph. Now, could we have the next photograph given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P109.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can you tell us what's in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows the garages belonging to Betonirka, the Betonirka compound where we were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you kept in one of those garages?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in garage number 3. But may I take it in turn from the entrance. This was garage 1, garage 2, and garage 3, and I was in this third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were moving from right to left on the photograph. So garage number 3 is the one on the left?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the entrance, taking it from the entrance. That's right, yes.
