utterances.text: May I just add that I gave it of my own free will, of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Karabeg, yes. Now -- and I also understand that, I think, back in 1997 you also gave a statement, but that wasn't signed. That was more or less along the lines of an outline of your evidence. That was, I think, taken by the Prosecutor, Ms. Brenda Hollis. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you remember how long that particular one took, the 1997 one?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But nevertheless, getting back to your 1999 statement, and in fact any statement you give to a legal authority, you as a lawyer are aware of the importance of telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? That basically goes without saying, doesn't it, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, I think you've still got your statement before you. No, I don't think you have. The statement from 1999 with the paragraphs outlined and numbered. Okay. So, Mr. Karabeg, you're aware of the importance of statements as a lawyer as -- in terms of their purposes for investigations and for finding relevant people responsible. You're aware of all of that, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. You'd agree with me, Mr. Karabeg, that nowhere in your statement is the name Krajisnik mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if we go specifically to your paragraph 11 -- sorry, paragraph 12 of your statement -- have you got that paragraph before you, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What you've written there is that: "In early April 1992, Vrkes said in the Assembly sessions that there was a lot of pressure about this matter from the leadership of Banja Luka. He did not mention any names."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even think that this might not be correctly translated, because he wouldn't have mentioned Vrkes had that been that, because we were linked with respect to the purchase of an apartment and were supposed to have a meeting. He was buying an apartment from a friend of mine, and I just happened to ask him by and by, "Why are you putting that on the agenda?" And then he happened to mention that. So I said I didn't attach any particular importance to it at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. But the fact is, Mr. Karabeg, that when you gave your statement, aware as you are of the importance of ensuring all relevant information as a lawyer, what you've got in your statement is that he did not mention any names?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He did not mention any names in the Municipal Assembly meetings. It doesn't refer to a private conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think it would have been more appropriate to say whether Ms. Loukas could further explore under what circumstances he said this and then it would have come out rather than to have a kind of a debate on what happened or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, might I be allowed to elaborate? From late March and April 1992, the SDS had previously insisted that the Sanski Most municipality belonged to Republika Srpska and they be joined to the centre region of Banja Luka. The Serbs at the beginning wanted the whole -- the entire municipality to be part of the RS. In early April 1992, Vrkes said in the Assembly sessions that there was a lot of pressure about this matter from the leadership of Banja Luka. He did not mention any names. Nobody ever said he mentioned any names at the Assembly meeting. We were deciding to meet with Vrkes after the Assembly meeting privately, and that's when he said that to me, when he mentioned that. So he didn't mention it at the Assembly session, and this refers to the Assembly session, that last Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the Chamber would have preferred that this testimony would have been introduced in a different way rather than the way it was done, Ms. Loukas -- yes, Mr. Hannis, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I apologise, but this specific question and this answer that he just talked about was given in the cross-examination that's been tendered to you in the written form, so I'm not understanding why it was necessary to do it now. Page 6272, lines 14 through 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, getting back --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, I understand that your answer is that what you're stating there in your statement is that he did not mention any names and your explanation is that you're saying he did not mention any names in the Assembly sessions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course, you didn't say that in your statement. You don't say, "He did not mention any names in the Assembly sessions," do you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says so here. "Vrkes said in the Assembly sessions that there was a lot of pressure about this matter from the leadership of Banja Luka. Did he not mention any names." That's what it says, full stop. At the Assembly sessions he would say. At the Assembly sessions he said. That's what it says. So nobody says that he mentioned any names, named any names at the Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Karabeg, you've already conceded that you know the importance as a lawyer of putting in everything you know. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: If I were to give statements about what happened and evolved and took place, it would take me half a year to make this statement, not one or two days. And in learning new things, I would always amend and change my statements and add on to them in light of what I learned subsequently. So I'm quite conscious that I have to say the truth. I am fully conscious of the fact that I am here to tell the truth, and I'm fully conscious of where I'm sitting here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather not have a debate between counsel and the witness. Ms. Loukas, your last question about putting in everything you know, wasn't it still about during the meeting or outside the meeting? I'm not -- it's not perfectly clear to me. That was your question, your last question. Was this still about the issue we discussed before about whether this point about -- well, the -- that it would have been proper to add that he did not mention any names, to add to that that it was not -- well, the context is clear enough, I would say, if you would have to -- if you describe an occasion and if you have to repeat in every single sentence that the new sentence relates to the situation you described in the previous sentence, then I would say it would be improper to ask a witness whether this was not a -- neglecting his duty to say everything. So therefore, if that was the issue --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, that wasn't actually the issue, Your Honour. I'm actually approaching it from a different angle now. If that wasn't apparent from the question, then I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honour. Should I keep --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could finish this one or two questions and then have a break until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, you're a lawyer and you know the importance of ensuring that when you give a detailed statement to investigators who are trying to find relevant people, evidence in relation to relevant people who might be responsible, that it's important to include as much as you know. You would fairly have to concede that. That's the case, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you said in your statement, "He did not mention any names," that of course was the appropriate opportunity to say, "By the way, though, outside the Assembly session he mentioned some names because we had a private conversation." You'd have to fairly concede that as well, would you not, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a robot and remember everything in the most minutest of details and to tell you all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's an appropriate juncture at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, do you have any idea of how much time you'd still need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course it doesn't depend entirely on me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the witness does tend to answer, as we've seen from his evidence in chief and partly from his cross-examination, in a rather longer fashion than one might expect, but then again we're all lawyers and we understand that tendency. So, Your Honour, I would have thought certainly no longer than an hour as an absolute maximum. And I hope I'm not being too sanguine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karabeg, we'll continue tomorrow morning, 9.00, and I take it in the same courtroom, Madam Registrar. Madam Registrar confirms that by nodding, which is a certainty for the Chamber. We would like to see you again. May I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given and still about to be given. Mr. Hannis, any issue you'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, I would like to advise the Court that both parties outside of court are trying to work on, trying to agree to some things that would shorten the trial or speed the trial, and in connection with that I have been asked to renew my inquiry about scheduling for the week of June the 7th by people who are arranging travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I told the parties before, the Chamber was unable to give any decision not being informed about any progress made, but the Chamber interpreted the absence of Mr. Stewart as a signal that the parties might meet outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour's interpretation of signals is finely tuned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Loukas. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
